Hi Elena — Vivek here from infra/serving. I'll keep this concrete. Below are our standard hosted metering rules and three short examples that match your csv. All numbers are illustrative but reflect our production metering logic.

Metering rules (hosted API):
- Input tokens: any bytes submitted to the model as part of the request (role: system, user, assistant when provided, and tool inputs if you pass them as text into the model).
- Output tokens: any text the model generates as the response (including texts emitted during a tool call).
- Tool returns are billed as output on the call that generated them. If you subsequently include that returned text in a new model call, those tokens are billed again as input on that new call. There is no automatic de-duplication across distinct API calls.
- Rounding: token counts are integer token counts (we tokenize with our BPE variant). For billing we round up to the nearest whole token (i.e., fractional tokens don't exist). We do not round to higher billing granularity (no per-request minimum in tokens), but billing is aggregated per invoice period where applicable for discounts. Streaming: tokens are accounted as they're generated; if a call is cancelled mid-stream you are billed for tokens generated up to cancellation.

Examples (from your csv):
1) Single chat with system prompt
- System prompt: 18 tokens
- User message: 34 tokens
- Model response: 76 tokens
Billing: input=18+34=52 tokens, output=76 tokens. Total billed = 128 tokens for that request.

2) Tool call flow (search tool)
- Call A (model decides to call tool): prompt to model (system+user+tool schema) = 60 input tokens
- Model triggers tool; tool returns a 24-token snippet (tool return is emitted by the model runtime while honoring tool format)
- Call A output billed = 24 tokens (tool output)
- Call B (you feed tool snippet back as user context to synthesize final answer): input for Call B = 24 (tool text) + 12 (user follow-up) = 36 tokens; model generates 48 tokens
Billing: Call A billed input=60, output=24. Call B billed input=36, output=48. Total billed across both calls = 168 tokens.

3) Streaming + cancellation
- Single call streamed; model generated 92 tokens before client cancel; we bill for the 92 output tokens generated, plus whatever input tokens were submitted at the start. If the model buffers partial tokens at the encoder/decoder level, the runtime counts only completed tokens that are emitted to the client.

Notes on potential optimization to reduce double-counting:
- If you do search+generate in a single call (model performs retrieval and synthesizes without separate tool handoff), then the retrieval text becomes part of model-generated output rather than a standalone tool return; that may reduce duplicate billing but requires prompt engineering.
- Caching: Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments can cache tool results at the prefix/KV level to avoid repeated model invocations; hosted customers can request a recommendation from Redwood Optimize to reduce repeat tool calls.

Hi Elena — Monica from pricing. Based on the illustrative token counts Vivek provided and the traffic profile you sketched in the SOW (avg 35k chat requests/day, 12% tool-invocation rate), here's a concise delta to map to the draft commitment tiers:

Baseline hosted rate: $0.0040 per 1k input tokens, $0.015 per 1k output tokens (example ratecard line in attached PDF).
Assumed monthly volume (example): 1,000,000 input tokens; 2,200,000 output tokens.
Gross monthly charge (no discount): 1,000 * $0.0040 + 2,200 * $0.015 = $4 + $33 = $37 (example math scaled).
Discounting: Under the proposed 12-month committed tier (ACME-12M), we would apply a 28% discount to compute a net effective price. That yields net monthly ~$26.64 in the worked example.

Rounding impact: Because we bill at integer tokens and your per-request counts are typically tens to hundreds of tokens, the rounding-to-integer rule has negligible effect on the monthly total (<0.2% in our sensitivity runs). The primary double-counting risk is tool-return re-ingestion; the ways to mitigate are: single-call synthesis, caching, or having Redwood manage the orchestration so we can apply prefix caching.

If you'd like, we can (A) produce a 90-day projected invoice sample under ACME traffic to validate the math, and (B) include a SOW clause that defines tool-return handling (so both sides agree how multi-call flows will be architected).
